subtype: Approach: working backward from exam dates and syllabus weight [Thinking]
passage: Voice note for Rafiq, from Pema. You asked how I even started on boards, so listen. First I counted backwards starting from the exam in March, week by week, and found I had about twenty-two weeks. Then I wrote every chapter of every subject beside its marks weightage from the syllabus sheet. That was the surprise: Science and Maths hold the biggest share, and I had been giving Social Science the same time as them. So I gave the early mornings, when my head is clear, to Science and Maths, and moved the lighter subjects to the evening. I taped the count of weeks over my desk. It does not make the syllabus smaller, but now it looks like a mountain with steps.

qa.q: How many weeks did Pema count before the March exam?
What did Pema feel on discovering the marks weightage?
qa.a: Surprised, and probably a little worried, because time had been spread evenly while the marks were not.

qa.q: What could Pema do if early mornings stop working?
qa.a: Review after a week and move the hard subjects to another clear-headed time, because the plan should follow energy.

qa.q: How might Rafiq see Pema's plan?
qa.a: As clear and useful because it turns a big syllabus into steps, though Rafiq may wonder whether early mornings would suit everyone.

grounding: A Class 10 student counts backwards from the exam date, ranks chapters by marks weight and gives the most hours to Science and Maths.

passage: Jyoti shares a desk lamp with me in the hostel, so I watched the whole thing on Sunday night. She pinned a calendar to the wall and drew a red circle round 3 March, the first board paper. Then she counted backward, tapping each week with her pen. "Sixteen weeks. Not twenty. Sixteen." Next she opened the marking scheme and wrote every chapter on a sheet with its marks beside it. Nazia from the next room leaned in the doorway and asked why she was wasting time on lists. "Look," Jyoti said, pointing. "Science and Maths have the heaviest chapters, and they're my weakest. English I'm fine in. So those two get my mornings, five to seven, when my head's clear." I don't know if she was calm or scared underneath. Her pen was very steady, though. On Monday her alarm went off at a quarter to five.

qa.q: What date did Jyoti circle in red?
qa.a: She circled 3 March, the first board paper.

qa.q: What does Jyoti's steady pen suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt focused and in control while planning, though the narrator cannot tell whether she was calm or anxious underneath.

qa.q: What else could Jyoti add to the plan, and why?
qa.a: A spare week or two before March for revision or sick days, because a plan with no slack breaks at the first delay.

qa.q: Why might Nazia see the lists as a waste of time?
qa.a: Nazia may feel that only studying counts as progress, not yet seeing how the lists show where the hours matter most.

grounding: An observer watches a Class 10 student count back from the exam date, rank chapters by marks and give Science and Maths the early mornings.

passage:
10 November. Manoj sits on the floor with the exam datesheet and a school calendar. Maths on 11 March, Science on 18 March. He counts the weeks back from the first paper. Seventeen. Then he goes through the syllabus and writes the marks for each chapter beside it. "Chemistry and algebra carry the most, and they're my worst," he mutters. Leela Chechi, home from college, watches him circle them. "Then those get the mornings," he decides. "Five-thirty to seven-thirty, before anyone's awake."
14 January. The mornings are still dark and he still hates the alarm. But the chemistry chapter on acids is done, and he can explain it to Leela Chechi without the book.
11 March. Before leaving for the Maths paper he turns the plan over. On the back, in November handwriting: "Hardest first. Most marks first."

qa.a: The Maths paper was on 11 March.

qa.q: How did Manoj seem to feel about the early alarm by January?
qa.a: He still hated it and felt tired in the dark mornings, but he was probably quietly proud once he could explain acids without the book.

qa.q: What would you change first if Manoj fell behind in February?
qa.a: Redo the count from the new date, still putting the heaviest weak chapters first, instead of dropping the mornings altogether.

qa.q: What might Leela Chechi think while watching him circle the chapters?
qa.a: Leela Chechi may be impressed that he planned from the dates and marks, and later glad to see it working when he explains acids without the book.

grounding: Shows a Class 10 student counting back from the exam date and giving the heaviest, weakest subjects the early mornings.
